paragraphs.heading: What they were
paragraphs.text: The Punic Wars were three wars between the Roman Republic and the Carthaginian Empire, fought between 264 and 146 BC. Added together, they made forty-three years of fighting on land and sea across the western Mediterranean, plus a four-year revolt against Carthage. When they began, Rome and Carthage were the two leading powers of the western Mediterranean.

paragraphs.heading: Friends drifting into war
paragraphs.text: For a century before the first war, Rome had been pushing hard into southern Italy, and by 270 BC it held the whole peninsula south of the Arno River. Carthage, with its capital in what is now Tunisia, ran an empire built on the sea, a thalassocracy, covering southern Iberia, much of coastal North Africa, Corsica, Sardinia and western Sicily. The two states got on well, with strong trade ties and several formal pledges of friendship. But as their borders drew closer, the risk of clashes rose, and they slid into war more by accident than by plan.

paragraphs.heading: The first war
paragraphs.text: The First Punic War broke out on Sicily in 264 BC, when Rome's expansion ran into Carthage's hold on the island. Carthage had a wide empire at sea, while Rome had a strong army but no navy at all. The fighting centred on Sicily and the waters around it and dragged on for twenty-three years, until Carthage was beaten in 241 BC. Carthage paid heavy reparations, and Sicily became Rome's first province.

paragraphs.heading: Hannibal in Italy
paragraphs.text: The Second Punic War began in 218 BC, when the Carthaginian general Hannibal crossed the Alps and invaded mainland Italy. His army did well at first and stayed in Italy for fourteen years. Rome's invasion of Carthage's African homeland in 204 BC forced his recall, and he lost the battle of Zama in 202 BC. The peace of 201 BC took Carthage's overseas lands, charged it a large indemnity, cut its forces and banned it from going to war without Rome's say-so, so it stopped being a military threat.

paragraphs.heading: Carthage destroyed
paragraphs.text: In 151 BC Carthage tried to defend itself against Numidian encroachment, and Rome used this as grounds to declare war in 149 BC. The Third Punic War was fought only on Carthaginian soil, in present-day Tunisia, and centred on a siege of the city. In 146 BC the Romans stormed Carthage, killed or enslaved its people and levelled it completely. Its lands became the Roman province of Africa, and the ruins lie east of modern Tunis.

paragraphs.heading: How we know
paragraphs.text: The most trusted account comes from Polybius, a Greek taken to Rome as a hostage in 167 BC. Where he could, he questioned people from both sides, and he went with the Roman general Scipio Aemilianus to North Africa during the third war. Modern historians think he was too kind to Scipio and his family but still accept most of his account. Livy, a Roman historian who leaned heavily on Polybius, is openly pro-Roman and often wrong about battles. No source written from Carthage's side survives.
